[ZAJJAJ:v1p141#2/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · قوم | reports | Others treat “yukhriǧ lanā” as a supplication, equivalent to the direct request “Bring it out for us.”
[ZAJJAJ:v1p141#2/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | prefers | He prefers construing the following verb as the response to an imperative, as with “tell My servants to establish prayer”; Qur’anic imperatives without a jussive particle are otherwise indicative. | mentions 14:31, 61:11, 61:12
[ZAJJAJ:v1p143/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | Al-qithāʾ has two dialectal forms; some readers pronounce its possessive form with ḍamma, while the more common and better reading has kasra.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p143/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | prefers | “Fūm” means wheat, and more broadly baked grains; the proposed meaning “garlic” is unknown in Arabic and ill-suited to a request for staple food, since wheat is food’s foundation. “Fūmū lanā” means bake bread for us.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p143/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | prefers | The unhamzated reading “adnā” is preferred in transmission and means nearer or lower in value; the hamzated “adnaʾ” is also possible and denotes something base or vile.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p144/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Most readers include final alif in “miṣran”; it can mean any town, appropriate to their wilderness setting, or Egypt as a masculine proper name and is then declinable.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p144/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | A reading without alif can refer to Egypt: the place name is treated as masculine but named after a feminine city, so it is indeclinable, as in the cited verse. | mentions 12:99
[ZAJJAJ:v1p144/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | “Dhilla” is abasement and “maskana” is submission or humility; the latter derives from stillness, since poverty reduces a poor person’s movement.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p144/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The expression “bāʾū bi-ghaḍab” means that they bore or incurred the wrath.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p144/r5] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | “That” refers to the wrath that came upon them because they disbelieved in God’s signs.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p145/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · أهل المدينة | reports | The agreed reading of “nabiyyīn,” “anbiyāʾ,” and “barīʾa” drops hamza; a group of Medinan readers pronounce hamza in these forms throughout the Qur’an.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p145/r2] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | prefers | Dropping hamza is better: hamzated faʿīl forms usually pluralize as faʿlāʾ, whereas weak-root forms take afʿilāʾ; the latter pattern is possible with sound roots but rare.
[ZAJJAJ:v1p145/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | “Nabī” may derive from “anbaʾa,” with hamza dropped through frequent use, or from a verb meaning to rise, giving the sense of high rank.

[IBNABIHATIM:v1p124/r5] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddi says that after leaving the wilderness, the manna and quails were withdrawn and the Israelites ate vegetables.

[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p80#2/r1] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | The hamzated form of النبيين derives from informing or announcing, as in the cited expressions about reporting truth and naming the angels. | mentions 2:31
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p80#2/r2] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | The unhamzated form is supported by the heaviness of hamza in Arabic speech; the cited Prophetic wording and Quraysh's non-hamzating illustrate this.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p80#2/r3] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | The unhamzated form may derive from nabwa, an elevated place, because the Prophet reports from the exalted realm and conveys God's message.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p80#2/r4] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | Arabic often drops hamza in words whose origins contain it; the author gives النبي، الخابية، البرية، الذرية، and الروية as parallels.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p80/r1] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | The kasra reading of both hāʾ and mīm in عليهم reflects the hāʾ's proximity to yāʾ and the need to break the meeting of two sukūns.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p80/r2] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | The ḍamma reading of both letters preserves their original vowels: the pronoun was originally همو before the preposition.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p80/r3] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | A kasra on hāʾ with ḍamma on mīm combines yāʾ proximity with the mīm's original ḍamma, needed to avoid two sukūns.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p80/r4] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | holds | Al-Kisāʾī matches Ḥamza here but differs in أنعمت عليهم: there mīm stays still, avoiding a shift from yāʾ to ḍamma; here hāʾ returns to its original vowel before mīm is moved. | mentions 1:7
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p110/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Abu ʿAmr kasras the pronoun mīm because its underlying connected form ended in yāʾ; after deletion, the mīm resumes that original vowel when moved. | mentions 36:14
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p110/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | He treats Abu ʿAmr’s kasra like the original ḍamma of Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn ʿĀmir, preferring an original vowel to an added one. | mentions 36:14
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p110/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh’s vocative truncation of Rād retains its original vowel at a consonant meeting, an analogy al-Fārisī uses for Abu ʿAmr.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p110/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Vowel-following is not always productive analogy: some forms are transmitted, while it is regular in رد، عض، فر and apparently in مردفين.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p110/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Following kasra is already accepted on the mīm of an active-participle marker even though it obscures the pattern, making it still likelier on a pronoun marker.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p110/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Arabic allows vowel-following across an intervening consonant, as in أجوءك for أجيئك and منتن.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p112/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | In منحدر, the ḍamma follows the inflectional ḍamma, as in ابنم، امرؤ، أخوك، فوك، and ذو مال.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p112/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | أنبؤك can follow the inflectional ḍamma or the initial imperfect-prefix ḍamma, even across an intervening consonant.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p112/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · عبد الله بن أبي إسحاق | reports | Abū ʿUthmān reports through Maḥbūb and ʿĪsā that Ibn Abī Isḥāq read بين المرء وقلبه and said رأيت مرءا وهذا مرء. | mentions 8:24
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p112/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | rejects | The exceptional pronunciation هو يئبى does not refute the pattern because it is anomalous; يخطف has kasra to favor vowel-following.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p112/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو الحسن | reports | Abū al-Ḥasan explains يخطف by first kasrating خ for two sukūns, then matching the prefix yāʾ to that kasra.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p112/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو الحسن | reports | Abū al-Ḥasan reports from ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar that some Arabs give three-letter nouns beginning with ḍamma a heavy pronunciation.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p112/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Forms of فم show case-conditioned endings (فوك، فاك، فيك); ذو مال behaves similarly but ذو does not take a pronominal suffix.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p114/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | With a first-person suffix, فم ends in yāʾ in all cases because the following pronoun imposes kasra, unlike عصاي whose weak ending does not shift with case.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p114/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Following works alike when the triggering vowel is inflectional or built; the distinction does not change the pattern, as ابنم shows.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p114/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | rejects | The proposal that ابنم’s nūn follows an added mīm is unsound: امرؤ shows the same following without deletion, and مرء is also attested.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p114/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The contrasting forms غد and غدو show that فم’s alternating deletion and completion is not a general consequence of matching وزن.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p116/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Vowel-following has two types: a non-inflectional vowel follows another non-inflectional vowel, as in مغيرة، منتن، يعفر، and ظلمات.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p116/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | In the second type, a non-inflectional vowel follows an inflectional one, as in امرؤ، ابنم، فوك، أجوءك، and أنبؤك.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p116/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | rejects | The examples of فم undermine the claim that these words are inflected in two places; movement can follow either inflection or construction.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p116/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | rejects | The reversed pattern cited in the grammar book is too rare to establish a rule; comparison of inflection with building is likewise only an exceptional analogy. | mentions 4:11
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · حمزة | reports | Ḥamza moves the mīm in عليهم، لديهم، and إليهم with ḍamma, matching the pronoun hāʾ, which he also pronounces with ḍamma. | mentions 28:23
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Because Ḥamza gives hāʾ its underlying ḍamma, the mīm takes that original vowel rather than an added kasra; no reader with hāʾ-ḍamma kasras this mīm.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The same principle explains ذال in مذ اليوم: its original ḍamma is retained when the consonant is moved.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisāʾī joins Ḥamza in ḍamma on عليهم and لديهم, though they normally kasra this hāʾ outside the relevant environments.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Al-Kisāʾī and Ḥamza use two dialect forms, a choice that broadens and eases recitation and accords with the transmitted seven modes.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Other readings likewise take more than one dialect form, including variants in أنعام، تكملوا، and يألتكم. | mentions 6:37, 2:185, 49:14
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · النبي | reports | A transmitted prophetic report says the Qurʾān was revealed in seven modes, all healing and sufficient.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r8] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · نافع | reports | Nāfiʿ is reported to alternate between عليهمو and عليهم, another instance of using both dialect forms.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r9] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | rejects | The objection that transitional movement should not trigger ḍamma on hāʾ only challenges the reading under a different analysis; it does not touch his explanation.

[THALABI:v1p206/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The prophets killed unjustly include Isaiah, Zechariah, John, and the other prophets killed by the Jews.

[ZAJJAJ:v1p141#2/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · بعض النحويين | reports | Some grammarians supply an implied request: ask God and say, “Bring it out for us,” and then He brings it out for them.

[ZAJJAJ:v1p143/r1] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | reports | Al-qithāʾ has two dialectal forms; some readers pronounce its possessive form with ḍamma, while the more common and better reading has kasra.

[ZAJJAJ:v1p144/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | “Dhilla” is abasement and “maskana” is submission or humility; the latter derives from stillness, since poverty reduces a poor person’s movement.

[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p110/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Abu ʿAmr kasras the pronoun mīm because its underlying connected form ended in yāʾ; after deletion, the mīm resumes that original vowel when moved. | mentions 36:14
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p110/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | He treats Abu ʿAmr’s kasra like the original ḍamma of Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn ʿĀmir, preferring an original vowel to an added one. | mentions 36:14
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p110/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh’s vocative truncation of Rād retains its original vowel at a consonant meeting, an analogy al-Fārisī uses for Abu ʿAmr.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p110/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Vowel-following is not always productive analogy: some forms are transmitted, while it is regular in رد، عض، فر and apparently in مردفين.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p110/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Following kasra is already accepted on the mīm of an active-participle marker even though it obscures the pattern, making it still likelier on a pronoun marker.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p110/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Arabic allows vowel-following across an intervening consonant, as in أجوءك for أجيئك and منتن.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p112/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | In منحدر, the ḍamma follows the inflectional ḍamma, as in ابنم، امرؤ، أخوك، فوك، and ذو مال.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p112/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | أنبؤك can follow the inflectional ḍamma or the initial imperfect-prefix ḍamma, even across an intervening consonant.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p112/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · عبد الله بن أبي إسحاق | reports | Abū ʿUthmān reports through Maḥbūb and ʿĪsā that Ibn Abī Isḥāq read بين المرء وقلبه and said رأيت مرءا وهذا مرء. | mentions 8:24
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p112/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | rejects | The exceptional pronunciation هو يئبى does not refute the pattern because it is anomalous; يخطف has kasra to favor vowel-following.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p112/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو الحسن | reports | Abū al-Ḥasan explains يخطف by first kasrating خ for two sukūns, then matching the prefix yāʾ to that kasra.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p112/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو الحسن | reports | Abū al-Ḥasan reports from ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar that some Arabs give three-letter nouns beginning with ḍamma a heavy pronunciation.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p112/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Forms of فم show case-conditioned endings (فوك، فاك، فيك); ذو مال behaves similarly but ذو does not take a pronominal suffix.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p114/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | With a first-person suffix, فم ends in yāʾ in all cases because the following pronoun imposes kasra, unlike عصاي whose weak ending does not shift with case.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p114/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Following works alike when the triggering vowel is inflectional or built; the distinction does not change the pattern, as ابنم shows.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p114/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | rejects | The proposal that ابنم’s nūn follows an added mīm is unsound: امرؤ shows the same following without deletion, and مرء is also attested.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p114/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The contrasting forms غد and غدو show that فم’s alternating deletion and completion is not a general consequence of matching وزن.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p116/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Vowel-following has two types: a non-inflectional vowel follows another non-inflectional vowel, as in مغيرة، منتن، يعفر، and ظلمات.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p116/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | In the second type, a non-inflectional vowel follows an inflectional one, as in امرؤ، ابنم، فوك، أجوءك، and أنبؤك.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p116/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | rejects | The examples of فم undermine the claim that these words are inflected in two places; movement can follow either inflection or construction.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p116/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | rejects | The reversed pattern cited in the grammar book is too rare to establish a rule; comparison of inflection with building is likewise only an exceptional analogy. | mentions 4:11
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · حمزة | reports | Ḥamza moves the mīm in عليهم، لديهم، and إليهم with ḍamma, matching the pronoun hāʾ, which he also pronounces with ḍamma. | mentions 28:23
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Because Ḥamza gives hāʾ its underlying ḍamma, the mīm takes that original vowel rather than an added kasra; no reader with hāʾ-ḍamma kasras this mīm.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | The same principle explains ذال in مذ اليوم: its original ḍamma is retained when the consonant is moved.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisāʾī joins Ḥamza in ḍamma on عليهم and لديهم, though they normally kasra this hāʾ outside the relevant environments.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Al-Kisāʾī and Ḥamza use two dialect forms, a choice that broadens and eases recitation and accords with the transmitted seven modes.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Other readings likewise take more than one dialect form, including variants in أنعام، تكملوا، and يألتكم. | mentions 6:37, 2:185, 49:14
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · النبي | reports | A transmitted prophetic report says the Qurʾān was revealed in seven modes, all healing and sufficient.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r8] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · نافع | reports | Nāfiʿ is reported to alternate between عليهمو and عليهم, another instance of using both dialect forms.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p117/r9] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | rejects | The objection that transitional movement should not trigger ḍamma on hāʾ only challenges the reading under a different analysis; it does not touch his explanation.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p120/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Weak radicals remain deleted in forms such as رمت المرأة and لم يخف الرجل despite a vowel inserted for two sukūns; if that vowel counted, forms like لم يقولا would retain the radical. | mentions 73:2
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p120/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | rejects | The poetic restorations أجره الرمح and ولا تهاله are too rare to outweigh the ordinary evidence against counting the transition

[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p120/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Poetic deletion can restore an underlying form for metrical necessity, as ضننوا, although ordinary usage keeps the consonant.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p121/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | In اضرب الاثنين and اكتب الاسم, the imperative lām remains kasrated because movement of the article lām for two sukūns counts like its being still.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p121/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Although the article lām attaches closely and adds definiteness, it behaves like a separate element because it is not part of the word’s root, as in hesitation forms ألي.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p121/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Jussive حذف of nūn in لم يضربا and لم يضربوا shows that transitional movement is not counted like a stable vowel.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p121/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Identical consonants do not assimilate when the second is moved only for two sukūns, another sign that this movement is disregarded.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p121/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Ordinary ḍamma on wāw can permit its replacement by hamza, as in أقتت، أدؤر، and النئوور; the next argument tests transitional ḍamma.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p123/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Wāw is not replaced by hamza when its ḍamma is only transitional; reports that some do so are treated as mistakes.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p123/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | A non-obligatory vowel behaves like a transitional one: in رمتا and غزتا, the weak radical stays deleted as in رمت المرأة.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v1p123/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | prefers | For the poetic form لها متنتان خظاتا, al-Fārisī prefers the account of metrical restoration over deleting the dual nūn, since such deletion occurs with relatives.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p87/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · المسيبي وقالون | reports | Al-Musayyibī and Qālūn report that Nāfiʿ hamzas النبيّ forms throughout the Qurʾān except al-Aḥzāb 50 and 53, where adjacent same-type kasra hamzas meet. | mentions 3:79, 3:112, 3:68, 33:50, 33:53
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p87/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ورش عن نافع | reports | Warsh reports Nāfiʿ hamzas all forms but drops the second hamza when two meet, whether alike or different, as in the two al-Aḥzāb phrases. | mentions 33:50, 33:53
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p87/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · الباقون | reports | All remaining readers leave hamza out of these forms. | mentions 3:79, 3:112, 3:68
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p87/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو زيد | reports | Abū Zayd explains نبأت from moving from one land to another, but distinguishes this travel verb from the etymology of نبي.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p87/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Al-Fārisī derives نبي from نبأ, news, because a prophet reports from God, rather than from the travel verb.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p87/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | rejects | He rejects derivation from النباوة, or both proposed roots, because Sibawayh’s diminutive and the agreed forms تنبأ and النبيئة establish hamza as the root consonant.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v2p87/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Agreement on تنبأ مسيلمة and النبيئة shows that the root has hamza, despite both hamza and weak-letter readings in the transmitted forms.
[RUMMANI:v1p91/r1] RUMMANI, d. 384 · author | holds | The metaphor of striking humiliation upon them makes its imposition perceptible and suggests degradation, intensifying the rebuke and aversion from their condition.
[SULAMI:v1p61/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · قيل | reports | People fall into two groups: those freed from self-direction and content with God's decree keep increasing, while those left to their own choices remain tossed about until they perish.
[SULAMI:v1p61/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | The rebuke means they exchanged God's primordial choice for them for disobedient asking and desire; God's word does not change. | mentions 50:29
[SULAMI:v1p61/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · الواسطي | reports | Al-Wasiti says they abandoned manna and quails, which came without effort, for food that suited their appetites and ordinary nature.
[THALABI:v1p204/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · يحيى بن وثاب، وطلحة بن مصرف، والأشيب العقيلي | reports | These readers pronounce qiththāʾihā with ḍamma on qāf, a Tamim dialect.
[THALABI:v1p204/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · ابن عباس | reports | Fūm means bread; the Arabs say fūmū lanā to mean “bake for us.”
[THALABI:v1p204/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · عطاء وأبو مالك | reports | Fūm means wheat in an old language; the cited poem uses fūm in the context of farming.
[THALABI:v1p204/r13] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | An unnamed view takes fūm to mean all grains.
[THALABI:v1p204/r14] THALABI, d. 427 · الكلبي والنضر بن شميل والكسائي والمعرج | reports | These authorities take fūm to mean garlic; al-Muʿarrij cites a line by Ḥassān in which fūm is paired with ḥawqal as food.
[THALABI:v1p204/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسن | reports | The Israelites were people accustomed to leeks, onions, and lentils; they reverted to their bad former habits and craved familiar foods, so they rejected manna and quails.
[THALABI:v1p204/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Although manna and quail are two foods, the Arabs can describe two things with the singular “one”; he cites the pearls and coral verse, although they come only from the salt sea. | mentions 55:22
[THALABI:v1p204/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم | reports | They kneaded manna and quail together, making one food that they ate.
[THALABI:v1p204/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Fa-dʿu means “ask,” and lanā means “for us.”
[THALABI:v1p204/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | The common reading has qiththāʾihā with kasra on qāf.
[THALABI:v1p205/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | On the garlic interpretation, Arabs interchange fāʾ and thāʾ, as in alternate words for gum and a grave; ʿAbd Allāh’s codex reads “and its garlic.”
[THALABI:v1p205/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · الأعمش | reports | Miṣr means the Egypt ruled by Ṣāliḥ b. ʿAlī; the uninflected reading of al-Ḥasan and Ṭalḥa and the codices of ʿAbd Allāh and Ubayy support its being a proper name, though inflected for shortness.
[THALABI:v1p205/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The requested items are the plants of the earth.
[THALABI:v1p205/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Ḍuribat means “was imposed” or “made binding”; al-dhilla is abasement and humiliation, explained as the jizya, with a supporting verse. | mentions 9:29
[THALABI:v1p205/r13] THALABI, d. 427 · unidentified speaker | reports | An unidentified gloss identifies the term with al-kastibinj, a Jewish weight.
[THALABI:v1p205/r14] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Miskana means possessing poverty; people may look poor while wealthy. It can also mean humiliation and poverty of heart; miskīn derives from stillness and few movements.
[THALABI:v1p205/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A report from ʿAlī praises lentils as blessed and purifying, softening the heart and increasing tears; it says seventy prophets blessed them, with Jesus the last.
[THALABI:v1p205/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Ubayy’s codex reads atubaddilūn in place of atastabdilūn.
[THALABI:v1p205/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Adnā means lower, baser, and worse; khayr means nobler and better, so the rebuke asks why they exchange good for evil.
[THALABI:v1p205/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · الفراء عن زهير العرقي | reports | Zuhayr al-ʿAriqī is reported to read adnāʾ with hamza; the common reading omits hamza.
[THALABI:v1p205/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · some grammarians | reports | Some grammarians derive adnā from adwan by moving the nūn and changing wāw to yāʾ, as in awlā min al-wayl.
[THALABI:v1p205/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | The good and evil may refer to kinds of food, or to God’s choice for them as against their own choices.
[THALABI:v1p205/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · قتادة | reports | Miṣr means any one of the cities: had the verse meant the particular Egypt, it would be uninflected, as in the command to enter Egypt in Joseph’s story. | mentions 12:99
[THALABI:v1p205/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · الضحاك | reports | Miṣr means the Egypt of Moses and Pharaoh.
[THALABI:v1p206/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · الكسائي وغيره | reports | They gloss bawāʾū bi-ghaḍab as “returned.”
[THALABI:v1p206/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The prophets killed unjustly include Isaiah, Zechariah, John, and the other prophets killed by the Jews.
[THALABI:v1p206/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | A report says the Jews killed seventy prophets in one hour early in the day; 112 Israelite worshippers ordered right and forbade wrong, and were all killed by day’s end.
[THALABI:v1p206/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | “That was because they disobeyed and transgressed” means they went beyond God’s command and committed His prohibitions.
[THALABI:v1p206/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو روق | reports | Abū Rawq glosses the phrase as “deserved”; he considers the bāʾ an extra particle.
[THALABI:v1p206/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda says the phrase means they bore and acknowledged it, comparing it to the prophetic supplication “I acknowledge Your favor upon me and my sin”; God’s anger means blame, threat, and punishment, and likewise hatred and wrath.
[THALABI:v1p206/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Their unbelief in God’s signs concerns the description of Muḥammad as merciful in the Torah, Gospel, and Qurʾān.
[THALABI:v1p206/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | The common reading has yaqtulūn with light consonants; al-Sulamī reads it with shadda, expressing intensive killing.
[THALABI:v1p206/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | The famous reading has al-nabiyyīn with shadda and no hamza; Nāfiʿ alone uses hamza a

[THALABI:v1p206/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | Without hamza, the word may reflect deletion of hamza for ease because it is frequent, or mean elevated, from nabūʾa, as in the cited line about a side lifted from the bed.

[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p128#2/r10] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Al-dhilla can mean humiliation and abasement, or the imposition of jizya, the latter according to al-Hasan and Qatada.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p128#2/r11] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · أبي العالية | reports | Maskana may mean need, according to Abu al-ʿAliya, or poverty, according to al-Suddi.

[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p128#2/r13] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A report describes a man bringing his brother's killer to the Prophet, who says “he is equivalent to him,” meaning the killer takes the victim-killer's place.

[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p128#2/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Most reciters read miṣran with tanwīn; some read it without tanwīn, and Ibn Masud's reading omits the alif.

[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p128#2/r6] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan, Abu al-ʿAliya, and al-Rabi say the verse means the specific Egypt from which the Israelites left, Pharaoh's Egypt.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p128#2/r7] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Some derive miṣr from cutting off, as the city is bounded off by its built-up area.

[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p128#2/r9] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A line by ʿAdi ibn Zayd uses miṣran for what separates day and night, as lexical evidence.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p130/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · أبو إسحاق الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj derives bāʾū from equality: they were made equal in wrath.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p130/r10] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A third etymology derives nabī from elevation because prophets hold a high rank.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p130/r11] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Layla al-Akhyaliyya's verse uses bawāʾ for equivalence between slain parties, supporting the interpretation of bāʾū.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p130/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · عبادة بن الصامت | reports | A report from ʿUbada ibn al-Samit says the Prophet distributed spoils among them on an equal basis, illustrating bawāʾ as equality.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p130/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisaʾi says bāʾū means they returned with God's wrath; return must be accompanied by something good or evil.

[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p130/r6] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Nabī has the plural form nabāʾ, used by Abbas ibn Mirdas in a verse praising the Prophet.

[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p174#2/r4] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | The demonstrative refers to humiliation, indigence and incurring wrath, caused by disbelief and killing prophets; the Jews killed Isaiah, Zechariah, John and others.

[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p174/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Adnā means lower in rank and smaller in value; nearness and distance can metaphorically indicate low and high worth.

[KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p174/r6] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | If it means the country, it has only one of the two causes of indeclinability; if it means any city, it is indefinite, while Abdullah's codex and al-Aʿmash read the city name without tanwin.

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p153#2/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · علي بن سليمان | reports | Ali ibn Sulayman derives أدنى, with eased hamza, from danīʾ, meaning plainly base or inferior.

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p153#2/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The verse asks whether the Israelites would exchange the inferior herbs, cucumbers, fūm, lentils, and onions for the better manna and quail.

[TABRISI:2:61#2/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj rejects garlic as an implausible meaning because people would not ask for garlic without bread, the staple.

[TABRISI:2:61#2/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | ʿAdas means the familiar lentil grain.
[TABRISI:2:61#2/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Adnā can mean nearer or lower, as in something close or inferior.

[RAZI-FULL:v3p92/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A monotonous diet can weaken appetite and digestion; variety can strengthen appetite and increase pleasure, making a change of food reasonable.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p92/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Nothing in the Quran says they were forbidden to request a different food, and the response granting what they asked for indicates the request was permissible; otherwise answering it would entail prophetic sin.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p92/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | An objection says God gave them an immediate worldly request after they rejected what He chose, as in 42:20; Razi answers that this departs from the apparent meaning. | mentions 42:20
[RAZI-FULL:v3p92/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | An objection reads their inability to endure one food as proof they disliked the manna and quail, making the request sinful.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p92/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Razi replies that they expressed desire for another food, not dissatisfaction with what they had; the future negation in lan does not establish resentment toward the present food.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p92/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | An objection takes Moses' question about replacing better with inferior food as an explicit condemnation proving the request sinful.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The usual reading of ihbiṭū is with bāʾ kasra; another reading has bāʾ ḍamma.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The well-known reading gives Miṣran tanwin despite the two factors of definiteness and feminine gender because its middle consonant is quiescent, as with Nuh and Lut; if common noun, it has only one factor. | mentions 6:84, 6:86
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · عبد الله | reports | The codex of ʿAbd Allah and al-Aʿmash's reading have Miṣr without tanwin.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan says the final alif in miṣran was added by a scribe, making the word definite and referring specifically to Pharaoh's Egypt; this is also transmitted from Abu al-ʿAliya and al-Rabiʿ.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · مفسرون | reports | Among those accepting tanwin, some take Egypt to mean Pharaoh's country, while others understand it as any town where the requested foods could be found.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · كثير من المفسرين | reports | Many commentators deny that Miṣr means Pharaoh's Egypt, citing the command to enter the Holy Land, the grant of that land, the ban on turning back, and the forty-year exclusion before entry. | mentions 5:21
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | An objection says the command to enter the Holy Land may be recommendatory and therefore need not bar entry into Egypt; Razi invokes the principle that an imperative is presumptively obligatory. | mentions 5:21
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | One food means a single unchanging menu or manner of eating, not a single food species.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Adnā does not mean inferior in religious benefit, since God granted the request; it refers to worldly benefit.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93/r11] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The comparison does not rank the foods' taste universally, since a food delightful to one people may be inferior to another; it concerns the certainty and effortless availability of manna and quail versus the requested foods.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93/r12] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A counterargument says guaranteed food disliked by their tastes was harder to consume than desired food obtained with effort; Razi answers that certain present benefit still outweighs uncertain distant benefit.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The usual reading has qithāʾihā with qaf kasra; al-Aʿmash and Talha read it with qaf ḍamma.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The usual reading is fumihā with fa; a reading attributed to Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas has thumihā, which some consider more fitting beside onions.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عباس | reports | One report from Ibn ʿAbbas interprets fum as wheat.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عباس | reports | Another report from Ibn ʿAbbas interprets fum as bread; this is also transmitted from Mujahid, ʿAta, and Ibn Zayd, and Arabic usage includes fumū lanā meaning bake for us.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عباس | reports | Another view, also transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid, interprets fum as garlic; al-Kisaʾi selects this view.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Supporters of the garlic interpretation cite the Ibn Masʿud reading thumihā, argue that wheat could not be inferior to manna and quail, and note garlic's fit with lentils and onions.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The usual reading is atastabdilūna; Ubayy b. Kaʿb's codex has atubaddilūna with bāʾ quiescent.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p93/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · زهير الفرقبي | reports | Zuhayr al-Farqabi reads adnaʾ with hamza, from the word for baseness.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p94/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Even if entering the Holy Land were only recommended, allowing the prophets to abandon a recommended duty would be improper. | mentions 5:21
[RAZI-FULL:v3p94/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A reply says do not turn back can mean do not disobey the command or deny the Holy Land's superiority, or the prohibition may apply only for a specified time; Razi finds that limitation contrary to the apparent sense. | mentions 5:21
[RAZI-FULL:v3p94/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi says the context makes do not turn back refer to the immediately preceding order to enter the Holy Land, while restricting the prohibition to a particular time departs from its apparent meaning. | mentions 5:21
[RAZI-FULL:v3p94/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو مسلم الأصفهاني | reports | Abu Muslim allows Pharaoh's Egypt: without tanwin, Miṣr must be a proper name and that is the only city with this name; with tanwin, it could remain a proper name or mean any city, allowing a choice among cities.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p94/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو مسلم الأصفهاني | reports | Abu Muslim argues that God bequeathed Egypt to the Israelites, so they could not be forbidden from entering it; he cites the report that God made them inherit it. | mentions 26:57, 26:59
[RAZI-FULL:v3p94/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | An objection says owning a house does not always permit entry, as when a person observing mosque retreat owns a home; perhaps Israel's inheritance meant authority while the Holy Land command barred entry. | mentions 5:21
[RAZI-FULL:v3p94/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Abu Muslim's side answers that ownership normally entails unrestricted use, and barring entry contradicts that default without evidence.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p94/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفريق الأول | reports | The first group answers Abu Muslim that the standard reading is with tanwin and that the apparent general choice can be restricted to this specific city by their earlier evidence.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p95#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Their killing of prophets also makes them deserve the preceding punishment; disbelief in God's signs means ignorance and denial and does not itself include killing prophets.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p95#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | One answer to why the text says without right is that people may commit a wrong act believing it justified through a doubt, but these people knew their killing was wrong and did it anyway.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p95#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A second answer is emphatic repetition, as in 23:117, whose wording that an idol has no proof makes the added denial rhetorically emphatic. | mentions 23:117
[RAZI-FULL:v3p95#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A third answer distinguishes God's just taking of life from people killing without right, forestalling the objection that God also kills.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p95#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The definite phrase without the right refers to the recognized legal grounds for killing among Muslims, as in the Prophetic report listing three cases in which Muslim blood is lawful. | mentions 3:21, 3:112
[RAZI-FULL:v3p95#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | By contrast, the indefinite phrase without any right denies that there was any justification of any kind. | mentions 3:21, 3:112
[RAZI-FULL:v3p95#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The phrase that was because they disobeyed restates the cause in different words, like a master listing a servant's past offenses with varied rebukes.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p95#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | They transgressed means they acted unjustly, crossing from right into falsehood.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p95#2/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The punishment's causes are ordered excellently: first offenses against God through ignorance and denial, then killing prophets, then personal sins, and finally sins against others through aggression.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p95/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الفريق الأول | holds | The first group replies to Abu Muslim that property may be limited, as with pledged and leased property, so prior evidence overrides the default that ownership permits unrestricted use.
[RAZI-FULL:v3p95/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Razi answers the Muʿta

item.text: The notes cover several layers: the food request and its timing, competing senses of fūm and miṣr, readings and grammar, and the later account of punishment. I’m keeping those questions separate while collecting each source’s evidence.

[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#2/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Qithāʾ can form qithāʾī, is a wāw-root, and aqthaʾa can mean to feed people it.

[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#2/r13] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The f-th-ʾ root also means calming anger, tiring from running, or heat subsiding; the proverb says sour curdled milk calms anger.

[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#2/r17] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masʿūd reads thūmihā with thāʾ; the same reading is also related from Ibn ʿAbbās.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#2/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Asking someone to feed one a report means asking them to tell it; an imam's being asked to be fed means prompting him when he loses his recitation.

[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#7/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · عكرمة عن ابن عباس | reports | ʿIkrimah transmits Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation: a town among these towns.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#7/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · طائفة ممن صرفها | reports | Other grammarians who read the word with tanwīn still identify it as Egypt itself.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#7/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | The indefinite-town view cites the apparent order to enter a town and reports that they lived in Syria after the wandering; the Egypt view cites their inheritance of Pharaoh's lands.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#7/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الأخفش والكسائي | reports | Al-Akhfash and al-Kisāʾī permit tanwīn because the name is light like Hind and Daʿd, citing a poem that uses both case forms.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#7/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · سيبويه والخليل والفراء | reports | Sībawayh, al-Khalīl, and al-Farrāʾ reject that declension, reasoning that Zayd would not take tanwīn as a woman's name.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#7/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · غير الأخفش | reports | Another grammarian explains the tanwīn by saying the word means a place, making it declinable.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#8/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Mā is the object governed by inna in 'you have what you asked for.'
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#8/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Bāʾū means they returned and remained bound to the consequence; the root means return, including the prayer acknowledging and binding oneself to God's blessing.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#8/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Bawāʾ can mean returning retribution for blood or equal status in a matter, as poetry also describes return with captives and spoils.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#8/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Al-Qurṭubī says the meaning of divine anger has already been treated in the Fātiḥah. | mentions 1:7
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#8/r13] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Dhālika explains the cause: they disbelieved in God's book and prophets' miracles, including those of Jesus, John, Zechariah, and Muhammad, and killed prophets.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#8/r14] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan has a variant reading of yaqtulūn; another transmission from him matches the common reading.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#8/r15] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · نافع | reports | Nāfiʿ reads al-nabiyyīn with hamzah throughout the Qur'an except two verses in al-Aḥzāb, where he leaves it unlengthened and unhamzated; the other readers omit hamzah throughout.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#8/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن وثاب والنخعي | reports | Ibn Waththāb and al-Nakhaʿī read saʾaltum with kasrah on sīn; saʾalta and salta are both used, and yatasāwalan shows the wāw root.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#8/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Ḍuribat ʿalayhim means humiliation and poverty were imposed and decreed, an image compared to pitching tents; the verb can mean a judge imposed a penalty.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#8/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الفرزدق | reports | Al-Farazdaq's line to Jarīr uses ḍuribat for an affliction imposed and sealed by scripture.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#8/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Al-Qurṭubī glosses dhillah as abasement and maskanah as poverty, claiming that even a rich Jew displays poverty's dress, submission, and humiliation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#8/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الحسن وقتادة | reports | Al-Ḥasan and Qatādah explain dhillah as the obligation of paying jizyah.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#8/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjāj takes maskanah as submissiveness, deriving it from stillness because poverty reduces movement.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#8/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abū ʿUbaydah glosses dhillah as lowliness; maskanah is the verbal noun of miskīn.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#8/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الضحاك بن مزاحم عن ابن عباس | reports | Al-Ḍaḥḥāk transmits Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation of the people struck by humiliation and poverty as holders of tax-farming contracts.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#9/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The two exceptions to Nāfiʿ's hamzated reading are 33:50 and 33:53, where he reads without lengthening or hamzah because two kasrah hamzahs meet; other readers omit hamzah everywhere. | mentions 33:50, 33:53
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#9/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن عباس والحسن | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan say prophets not commanded to fight could be killed, while every prophet commanded to fight was victorious.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#9/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The second dhālika points back to and reinforces the first; bi in bimā marks cause, and al-Akhfash glosses it as 'because of their disobedience.'
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#9/r12] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash interprets bimā as 'because of their disobedience'; disobedience opposes obedience, while transgression exceeds limits, especially in injustice and sins.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#9/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The hamzated form derives from anbaʾa, 'inform': nabīʾ is an active participle, plural anbiyāʾ, with nabāʾ also attested as a plural.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#9/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · العباس بن مرداس | reports | Al-ʿAbbās b. Mirdās's praise of the Prophet as the seal of nabāʾ supports the hamzated form.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#9/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Those omitting hamzah either derive the word from the same root with a softened hamzah or from nabā yanbū, 'to rise'; nabwah is elevation.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#9/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Without hamzah, nabī can mean a path; a messenger is called nabī because people are guided by him as by a road.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#9/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · شاعر | reports | An unnamed poet uses nabī for a path on the ground, supporting the unhamzated lexical sense.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#9/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو علي | reports | A report where the Prophet rejects nabīʾ with hamzah and accepts nabī without it has a weak chain, according to Abū ʿAlī; the Prophet's uncorrected hearing of a hamzated poem also weakens it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#9/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | 'Without right' magnifies the enormity of the killing; it does not imply any prophet could deserve execution, since none did an act requiring it.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61#9/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | God's allowing disbelievers to kill prophets honors them and raises their rank, as with believers slain in God's cause; it is not abandonment.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The request occurred during the wandering, after they tired of manna and quail and remembered their former life in Egypt.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو خراش | reports | Abū Khirāsh's poetry uses ṭaʿm first for food and then for its s

[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The verb ṭaʿima means to eat or taste; it means 'taste' in 2:249 and 'eat' in 33:53. | mentions 2:249, 33:53
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan says they were people accustomed to leeks, onions, and lentils, and their appetites returned to their bad old habits.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | They called manna and quail one food though they were two because they ate one together with the other.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قيل | reports | Another view says the two foods repeated daily, so they were called one regular fare, like a person constant in one practice.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · قيل | reports | Another interpretation is that they could not bear universal prosperity, which left no one needing help; the passage says they were the first to use slaves and servants.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Ṭaʿām can mean anything eaten or drunk; Qur'anic 'taste' can include drinking wine, and honey as salwā would also be a drink. | mentions 2:249, 5:93
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Food can conventionally mean grain or dates specifically; Abū Saʿīd's report on zakāt al-fiṭr contrasts a measure of food with barley.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | In ordinary usage, a food market means the place where food is sold, not every place selling something edible or drinkable.
[QURTUBI-FULL:2:61/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | With fatḥah, ṭaʿm can mean what taste conveys or something desirable; with ḍammah it means food.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61#2/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Minor sins lead to major sins, just as minor acts of obedience lead toward greater acts.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61#2/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · قيل | reports | The repeated demonstrative stresses that their punishment resulted both from disbelief and killing and from their sins and transgression.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61#2/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · قيل | reports | Alternatively, the demonstrative refers to disbelief and killing, with bāʾ meaning ‘along with’; a singular demonstrative can cover multiple matters under a contextual singular expression or ellipsis.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61#2/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Rubaʾ's description of a cow uses a singular pronoun for multiple marks, illustrating that demonstratives and pronouns are not strictly marked for real number or gender; alladhī can likewise mean plural.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The single food they could no longer bear was manna and quails from the wilderness.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r10] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | A reading pronounces qiththā with ḍamma, a dialectal form.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r11] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | The speaker of ‘he said’ may be God or Moses.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r12] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Adnā means nearer in rank and lower in worth; spatial nearness is metaphorically used for baseness and distance for honor.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r13] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | A reading has adnaʾ, derived from lowliness.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r14] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The better food means manna and quails, superior in pleasure, benefit, and freedom from the need to work for food.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r15] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Ihbiṭū miṣran means descend from the wilderness to it; the verb describes entering a valley or leaving a higher place.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r16] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Miṣr can mean a great city; the word originally denotes a boundary between two things.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r17] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · قيل | reports | A reported interpretation takes Miṣr as Egypt; its treatment as a proper name is supported by nonnunation in Ibn Masʿūd's codex.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r18] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Another account derives the name from Miṣrātim and says it was Arabized.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r19] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Humiliation and poverty enveloped or clung to them like a canopy or plaster on a wall, as requital for ingratitude.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Its oneness means it did not vary or change, as in the expression that an emir's table has one food because its colors do not change.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r20] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Jews are generally humiliated and poor, either actually or by affectation for fear of increased jizya.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r21] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Bāʾū means they returned carrying anger or became deserving of God's anger; the idiom means someone is liable to be killed for another, and its root connotes equality.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r22] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The demonstrative points back to the humiliation, poverty, and incurring of anger.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r23] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | God's signs may mean miracles they experienced: the sea split, clouds shaded them, manna and quails descended, and springs burst from stone.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r24] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Alternatively, the signs are revealed scriptures, including the Gospel, Qurʾān, stoning verse, and the Torah's description of Muhammad.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r25] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | They killed Isaiah, Zechariah, John, and others without grounds even by their own standards; desire and worldly love drove them.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r26] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Their disobedience, persistence, and transgression led them into disbelief in signs and killing prophets.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Alternatively, it was one kind of food; though it suited people of luxury, the Israelites were farmers who longed for familiar fare.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | They ask Moses to petition his Lord on their behalf.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r5] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Yukhrij means to bring forth or make exist; its jussive form answers the petition because prayer causes the response.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The phrase about what the earth grows uses figurative attribution, putting the recipient in the agent's place, and min is partitive.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r7] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The listed crops explain the preceding phrase as a circumstantial clarification; another analysis treats them as an appositive with the preposition repeated.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r8] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Baql means plants grown by the earth; here it refers to the choicest edible greens.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:2:61/r9] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | Fūm means wheat, and can also mean bread, as in the phrase ‘bring us bread’; another view takes it to mean garlic.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The one food was manna and quail; it was called one because it did not change, as a person may call a daily unchanging menu one food despite its variety.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r10] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The things they requested are available in cities, not in the wilderness.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r11] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Humiliation and poverty surround and cling to them; Jews are subdued and poor either literally or by displaying poverty out of fear of an increased poll tax.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r12] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | They may be poor in fact or display poverty and humility from fear that the jizya will be doubled.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r13] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · حمزة وعلى | reports | Hamzah and al-Kisa'i have a distinct vocalization of the pronoun in عليهم; Abu Amr kasras both hā and mīm, while the other readers kasra the hā and damma the mīm.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r14] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abu Amr reads the pronoun with kasra on both hā and mīm; the remaining readers kasra hā and damma mīm.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r15] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | To incur God's anger means to become deserving of it, by analogy with one who is liable to be killed in return for an equal victim.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r16] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisa'i is reported to read the following word as حفوا.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r17] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The first that refers to the imposed humiliation, poverty and deserved anger.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r18] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Their unbelief and killing of prophets caused their punishment; the prophets killed by the Jews included Isaiah, Zechariah and John.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r19] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · نافع | reports | Nafi' pronounces the word for prophets with a hamza, as in its related forms.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | Alternatively, they considered manna and quail one kind because both were refined foods, while they wanted the vegetables and grains familiar to an agricultural people.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r20] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Nabī may derive from informing, as one who tells from God, or from rising; nubuwwa is an elevated place.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r21] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Killing them without right means even by their own standard; the Torah did not warrant their killing, and the phrase is a circumstantial accusative describing wrongful killing.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r22] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | The repeated that may refer to sins generally, or specifically to Sabbath transgression; alternatively unbelief and killing arose from persistent disobedience and excess that hardened their hearts.

[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r5] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Qiththa means cucumber.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r6] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · ابن مسعود | reports | Fum means either wheat or garlic; Ibn Masud's reading has thum, garlic.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r7] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Adna means lower in rank and lesser in value, while what is better is higher and nobler.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r8] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | Misr may mean any city, to which they descend from the wilderness, located between Jerusalem and Qinnasrin; the wilderness is twelve by eight farsakhs.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p46#2/r9] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | Alternatively, Misr means Pharaoh's Egypt; it is declined despite feminine and proper-name features because it means a town or has a quiescent middle consonant, like Noah and Lot.
[NASAFI-FULL:v1p48/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | reports | The final that may point to unbelief and killing prophets together with the other acts of disobedience.
[QASHANI:2:61/r1] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | The Israelites’ one food is spiritual nourishment through knowledge, gnosis, and wisdom.
[QASHANI:2:61/r2] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Their request to Moses means asking God to permit the soul’s base desires, low pleasures, stale amusements, and other ego-centered satisfactions.
[QASHANI:2:61/r3] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Egypt signifies the city of the body; humiliation is the condition following pursuit of desires and greed for possessions, while misery means lasting need and dwelling in the lower realm.
[QASHANI:2:61/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | Incurring divine wrath signifies deserving distance from and expulsion by God; their downfall follows from being veiled from His signs and manifestations.
[QASHANI:2:61/r5] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | On a second inward reading, killing the prophets means attacking the heart’s prophets without a sound warrant, through falsehood, disobedience to heart and intellect, and transgression against their guidance.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p353/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Ṭaʿām means whatever is eaten, analogously to ʿaṭāʾ for whatever is given, and is a generic noun.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p353/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Wāḥid means indivisible or something to which no second is added; waḥada/yahidu means to be alone.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p353/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Duʿāʾ is calling aloud by the name of the person invoked, from daʿā/yadʿū.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p353/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The hamza in inbāt is causative: the word means bringing out something whose nature is to grow.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p353/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن دريد | reports | Baql is a genus covering fresh growth eaten by people and animals; the land verbs mean that the land has become vegetated, and Ibn Durayd connects al-bāqillāʾ to it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p353/r15] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Qithāʾ is a generic noun whose singular is qithāʾa, with qāf either ḍamma or kasra; maqthaʾa means land rich in it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p353/r16] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl identifies qithāʾ as cucumber.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Al-Ṣalt’s verse groups fūm with onion among the people’s provisions, supporting the reported garlic interpretation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن قتيبة | prefers | Ibn Qutayba chooses the bread interpretation, supported by the cited poem using fūm as a verb for baking.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قطرب | reports | Quṭrub gives fūm three senses: an onion cluster, a large piece of meat, or a large mouthful.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another view identifies fūm as chickpea in a Syrian dialect; its seller is called fāmī, a nisba form from fūmī, like shahli and dahri.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | ʿAdas is the familiar lentil; ʿAdas is also a proper name and a command used to urge a mule.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Baṣal simply means onion.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r15] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Adnā may be the elative of dunūw, ‘nearness,’ from danā/yadnū.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r16] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأخفش | reports | ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān al-Akhfash derives adnā from danāʾa, baseness or poor quality, with hamza lightened to alif.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r17] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو زيد | reports | Abū Zayd records the hamzated forms danuʾa/yadnaʾu and danāʾa/danāʾ.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r18] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · غيره | reports | Another grammarian derives adnā from dūn, ‘lower in rank,’ as a transformed form of adwan, like awlā from wayl.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r19] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Miṣr means a city and may derive from milking a sheep completely, drawing everything from its udder.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الصلت | reports | Al-Ṣalt’s verse cites fūm and onion among the people’s provisions, supporting the garlic reading.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r20] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Miṣr can instead mean a boundary between two lands; Hajar writes bimuṣawrihā for its borders, and the poem depicts the sun as a boundary between day and night.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مؤرج | reports | Muʾarrij’s quotation of Ḥassān’s verse glosses its food words as fūm and onion.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Neither consonant substitution is productive: thāʾ may become fāʾ and fāʾ may become thāʾ, as in athāfī/athāthī.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو مالك وجماعة | reports | Abū Mālik and a group identify fūm as wheat; the cited Uḥayḥa ibn al-Jallāḥ poem speaks of cultivating it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · المبرد | reports | The wheat meaning is identified as Egyptian usage and is al-Mubarrad’s preferred interpretation; al-Farrāʾ calls it an ancient dialect.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن قتيبة، والزجاج | reports | Ibn Qutayba and al-Zajjāj say fūm means edible grains.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو عبيدة، وابن دريد | reports | Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn Durayd define fūm as an ear of grain; Abū ʿUbayda specifies that this is the Asad dialect.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p354/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Other reported definitions make fūm the grains used for baking or bread itself.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p356/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · غيره | reports | Another account says they tired of manna and quail, were told to descend to a city, and first encountered Jericho.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p373/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The Israelites were weary of the wilderness and repetitive food, distant from their familiar land and habits; they expressed impatience and asked Moses to petition God for them.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p373/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أكثر أهل الظاهر من المفسرين | reports | Most outward commentators regard the request as sinful because they disliked the manna and quail, Moses called their requested food inferior, and his question rebuked them.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p373/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abū Ḥayyān replies that saying they could not endure one food shows a desire for other foods, not necessarily dissatisfaction with what God provided; a rebuke may concern forfeiting worldly or afterlife benefit.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | One explanation follows the singular grammatical form of ṭaʿām, not the fact that it refers to two foods.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · بنو عامر | reports | The Banū ʿĀmir dialect pronounces the command fa-dʿi with kasra on the ʿayn, treating daʿā as a weak verb like ramā-yarmī.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The Israelites asked Moses to pray because a prophet’s prayer was more likely to be answered; saying your Lord reflects his special closeness through conversation and revelation of the Torah.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | They said your Lord because God had specially favored Moses through intimate speech and giving him the Torah, so they hoped He would answer Moses’s prayer for them.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Yukh r ij is jussive as the response to the command udʿu, parallel to the response in the verse about fulfilling God’s covenant. | mentions 2:40
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another grammatical analysis supplies an omitted command, ask Him to bring the foods forth, with yukh r ij responding to that command.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r15] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · بعضهم | reports | Some say yukh r ij is jussive under an unexpressed lām of command; Basran grammarians do not allow this analysis.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r16] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh takes min in مما تنبت الأرض as partitive, with an omitted object of yukh r ij meaning something edible from what the earth grows.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r17] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash takes min as redundant and mā as a relative pronoun with an omitted object pronoun, a deletion that meets the required conditions.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r18] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · بعضهم | reports | Some take mā as a verbal noun, meaning from the earth’s growing.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r

19] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abū al-Baqāʾ rejects the verbal-noun analysis because an omitted concrete object cannot be described by a verbal noun; saying the earth grows is figurative, since God causes growth and the earth only receives it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd says the Israelites mixed manna and quail, making them like one color that combines several things.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another explanation says they received manna alone for a period, became tired of it, and then received quail alone and tired of that.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Some take the one food to mean quail, since manna was a drink or sweet accompaniment and only quail counted as food to them.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Others compare calling two foods one to calling one source two, as in the verse about pearl and coral coming from two seas although they come only from the salty sea. | mentions 55:22
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another view says they spoke while only one of the two foods was being sent down.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another interpretation says they meant they could not endure everyone being wealthy and no one needing to serve another; the one food represents their common status in the wilderness before social differences returned.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The author counts nine reported explanations for one food, including the two explanations attributed to al-Zamakhsharī on the preceding page.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374#2/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Fa-dʿu lanā rabbaka means ask your Lord for us; the object of the prayer is omitted and understood as asking Him to produce the requested foods.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Their request was permissible: the earlier eat-and-drink command was permission, so people allowed different foods may reasonably ask for another kind directly or through a messenger.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | They asked Moses because a prophet’s prayer is more likely to be answered; they had eaten the same food for forty years, were unused to it, and preferred familiar foods even when inferior.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | They may have sought other foods to leave the wilderness, where those foods were unavailable; variety also improves appetite and digestion compared with a single repeated food.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Because replacing one food kind with another is a reasonable aim and the Qurʾān does not say they were forbidden to ask, the request cannot be treated as sinful.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The response, descend to a town and you will have what you asked, confirms that the request was granted; granting a sinful request would be impermissible for prophets.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhsharī explains one food as the unchanged manna and quail, which they called one because it did not vary from day to day.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p374/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Another explanation is that manna and quail were one class of luxurious fare, while the Israelites as agricultural people wanted familiar varied crops and vegetables.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p375/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The phrase من بقلها is an appositive to مما تنبت الأرض with the preposition repeated, a fluent construction.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p375/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس والحسن وقتادة والسدي | reports | They interpret فومها as wheat.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p375/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another interpretation takes فومها to mean all grains.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p375/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مجاهد وابن عطاء وابن زيد | reports | They interpret فومها as bread.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p375/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another interpretation takes فومها to mean chickpeas.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p375/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | A final interpretation takes فومها to mean a grain ear or spike.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p375/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Both occurrences of من are partitive and attach to يخرج, either directly or through an estimated repeated verb; the latter analysis is standard.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p375/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abu al-Baqa allows من بقلها to explain the kind and treats it as an accusative circumstantial phrase from an omitted pronoun.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p375/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · المهدوي وابن عطية | reports | Al-Mahdawi and Ibn Atiyya call من بقلها an appositive even though they take the two prepositions to have different senses.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p375/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | The appositive analysis fails if the first من is partitive but the second is explanatory, since the two particles then differ in meaning.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p375/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | He prefers taking both particles as partitive; his school rejects the explanatory sense of من here and reinterprets its evidence.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p375/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | The greens mean choice vegetables people eat, such as mint, celery, and leek.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p375/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · يحيى بن وثاب وطلحة بن مصرف | reports | They read وقثائها with a ḍamma on qāf, which is an established dialect form.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p375/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | One interpretation takes فومها as garlic; Ibn Masud's ثومها reading supports it and fits the neighboring foods.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p376/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The listed foods span hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities: greens vary, cucumber is cold and moist, garlic hot and dry, lentils cold and dry, and onion hot and moist unless cooked.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p376/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · زهير الفرقبي | reports | Zuhayr al-Farqabi, also called Zuhayr al-Kisa'i, reads أدنأ with hamza.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p376/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | This sequence of five foods follows their differing temperamental qualities.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p376/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The pronoun in قال most naturally refers to Moses.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p376/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The pronoun could instead refer to God, supported by the ensuing command and promise.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p376/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The interrogative hamza in أتستبدلون expresses denial, and istibdāl means taking something in exchange.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p376/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبي | reports | Ubayy reads أتبدلون; the wording is figurative because God alone effects the change, but their request makes them seem to change it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p376/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | In the construction, الذي is the object and denotes what is gained, while the item introduced by باء is what is given up.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p376/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | On the Basran analysis, هو أدنى is the relative clause and أدنى its predicate; the comparison phrase من ذلك الطعام الواحد is omitted because the comparative is predicative and its counterpart follows.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p376/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | الذي is singular because it points back to the food and to ما in مما تنبت; agreement with the appositive would instead require a feminine plural.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p377/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | A commentator mistakenly split Zuhayr al-Kisa'i into two people when attributing the anomalous reading; Zuhayr al-Kisa'i and al-Farqabi are one man.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p377/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Zuhayr's hamzated reading derives أدنأ from lowliness; the unhamzated form may also have originated with hamza and been softened.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p377/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | If أدنى arose by metathesis from أدون, both forms mean lowliness and make a better contrast with خير; if it means nearer, its opposite is farther.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p377/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The omitted comparison after خير is منه, referring back to الذي هو أدنى; both relative clauses are nominal to express unbounded states, while the verbal clause مما تنبت suits recurring growth.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p377/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزجاج | reports | The first explanation measures superiority by value: vegetables are of little worth beside the more valuable manna and quails.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p377/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | prefers | Al-Zamakhshari chooses the value reading, glossing أدنى as lower in rank and less in worth; nearness can figuratively mean small value.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p377/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | A second explanation says manna and quails were God's gift and commanded food, so continuing to obey and thank Him earned reward in the afterlife, unlike the requested food.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p377/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | A third explanation grounds the comparison in taste and pleasure: manna and quails are better tasting than the vegetables requested.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p377/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | A fourth explanation values freedom from toil: manna and quails came without labor, while crops required cultivation and care.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p377/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | A fifth explanation values lawful purity: manna and quails came from God free of the defects, usurpation, unlawful elements, and doubts tha
