[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p377/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | A sixth explanation says manna and quails are superior in the kind of nourishment and benefit they provide.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p377/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The six explanations locate superiority in value, obedience and reward, pleasure, effort, lawfulness, or the kind of food.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p378/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | If Moses said أتستبدلون, the narrative omits that he prayed and God answered before the command هبطوا.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p378/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash explains declension despite proper-name and feminine status by the word's lightness from a still middle consonant.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p378/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari compares مصر, when treated as a proper name, to Nuh and Lut, which are declined despite foreignness because they are short with a still middle consonant.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p378/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | هبطوا مصرا can mean settle in a city; هبط منه means leave it, as though a person arriving in a town descends upon it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p378/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | A reading with ḍamma on the bāʾ in اهبطوا is another dialect form; kasra is more eloquent.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p378/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الحسن وطلحة والأعمش وأبان بن تغلب | reports | They read مصر without tanwin, as also written in the codices of Ubayy, Ibn Masud, and some Uthmanic copies; most readers give it tanwin.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p378/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قتادة والسدي ومجاهد وابن زيد | reports | With tanwin, مصر can mean any unspecified city, supported by the command to enter a town, later settlement in Syria, and the need for cities to obtain the foods requested. | mentions 2:58
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p378/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | The tanwin may still indicate an unspecified city, specifically one among the cities of the Holy Land, as supported by the command to enter the Holy Land. | mentions 5:21
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p378/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | An indefinite مصر may refer specifically to Pharaoh's Egypt, using an indefinite noun for a known person or place, as in asking for a man while meaning Zayd.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p378/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مالك | reports | Malik identified the place as Egypt, the speaker's town where Pharaoh lived, in a report transmitted by Ashhab.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p378/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · المعربون والمفسرون | reports | Some grammarians and exegetes allow the tanned مصر to be a proper name, explaining its declension by its lightness or by treating it as a place noun. | mentions 10:87
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p379/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Abu Hayyan says foreignness only blocks declension in names longer than three letters, so a three-letter name with a still middle consonant is declined.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p379/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · إبراهيم النخعي ويحيى بن وثاب | reports | They read سألتم with a kasra on the initial sīn, a form produced by overlap between two verb patterns for سأل.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p379/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The verb has a hamza-root pattern and a wāw-root pattern; يتساولان, analogous to يتجاوبان, supports the latter.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p379/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عيسى بن عمر | reports | Isa ibn Umar allowed مصر to be diptote by analogy with Hind, but this is unattested from Arabs except in the declined form, so the author rejects the analogy.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p379/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | The proposed diptote form rests on analogy to a disputed case and conflicts with Arabic usage, so it must be discarded.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p379/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الحسن بن بحر | reports | Hasan ibn Bahr says مصر means Jerusalem: although indefinite in form, it refers to a specific place.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p379/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The un-tanwined reading مصر means the proper name of Pharaoh's land.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p379/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · بعض الناس | reports | Some reject Pharaoh's Egypt because the Israelites left it, refused to fight the giants in the Holy Land, wandered for forty years and died, while their descendants entered Syria and later returned to Jerusalem; no exegete or historian says the wanderers went to Egypt. | mentions 5:21, 5:24
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p379/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | He summarizes four tanwin interpretations: an unspecified city anywhere, an unspecified Syrian city, Jerusalem as a specific place, or Pharaoh's Egypt.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p379/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | فإن لكم ما سألتم answers the imperative like a jussive clause; grammarians dispute whether اهبطوا implies a conditional or has an omitted condition.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p379/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The construction omits both a locative link, فيها, and the pronoun in سألتموه, with the conditions for ellipsis satisfied.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p380/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · شاعر | reports | The cited poetic form سأيلتهم is analyzed as the hamzated ساءلتهم with a yāʾ substitution; the poet combines the substitute with the hamza it replaces under metrical pressure.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p380/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن جني | reports | Ibn Jinni offers another account: hamza in سألتم became yāʾ as in a cited line, then the sīn was kasrated before yāʾ and the speaker restored hamza.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p380/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The request refers to the vegetables and grains they chose over manna and quails.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p380/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another interpretation takes the request to mean their reliance on managing their own livelihoods and food supplies.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p381/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | If باء means return, its preposition marks accompanying state; if it means deserve, the preposition completes the verb; if it means settle or become equal, it is locative, with different attachment analyses.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p381/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | ذلك may point to the punishment of wrath, or to the blow of humiliation and poverty.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p381/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | In ذلك بأنهم, ذلك is the subject, the following prepositional phrase its predicate, and باء marks cause: this happened because they disbelieved and killed.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p381/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | God's signs may mean Moses's nine miracles and others, the Torah, selected Torah passages, the Qur'an, or all signs revealed to the messengers.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p381/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The signs are attributed to God because they originate from Him.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p381/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The prophets they killed included John, Isaiah, and Zechariah.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p381/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash takes the preposition as causal and attached to باء, with an omitted object: they deserved punishment because God was angry with them.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p381/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The verb باء is used with good outcomes as well as evil ones, contrary to the claim that it occurs only for evil. | mentions 29:58, 10:93, 39:74
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p381/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · بعض الناس | reports | Some claim باء is used only in evil contexts.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p381/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | A Prophetic supplication uses باء for both a blessing and a sin, confirming the two usages.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p381/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Wrath here can mean the worldly calamities and punishments that befell them or punishment awaiting them in the afterlife.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p381/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | باءوا may carry a present-tense sense, as in other expressions where an impending event is stated in the past tense. | mentions 53:57, 54:1
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p381/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | من الله may attach to باءوا if باء means return, suggesting they turned away from God through disobedience; alternatively it adjectivally describes غضب, the clearer analysis with the meanings deserve or settle.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p381/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Describing the wrath as being from God magnifies and exalts its seriousness.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p382/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن مسعود | reports | A report from Ibn Masud says the Israelites killed seventy prophets; another version says three hundred in the morning, with killings openly active by evening.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p382/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · علي | reports | Ali's doubled-consonant reading يقتّلون intensifies the sense of repeated killing.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p382/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الحسن | reports | Hasan reads وتقتلون with second-person address, an instance of turning to address; another report gives the common third-person reading.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p382/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | When definite, النبيين and الأنبياء do not differ in meaning; without the article, the sound plural suggests few and the broken plural suggests many.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p382/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · نافع | reports | Nafi hamzates forms of نبي; Qalun replaces and assimilates the hamza in two connected readings in al-Ahzab, while most readers omit hamza. | mentions 33:50, 33:53
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p382/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | بغير الحق attaches to وتقتلون and is either a circumstantial phrase or a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun; both analyses are emphatic.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p382/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The wording does not imply any prophets were killed justly: prophets cannot deserve exec

ution; the qualification shames and condemns the killers, who claimed no justified basis even by their own standard.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p382/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another explanation treats the phrase as emphatic because no prophet ever brought anything warranting death; those killed were hated, and their killing raised their rank.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p382/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس وغيره | reports | Ibn Abbas and others say prophets not commanded to fight were killed, while every prophet commanded to fight was victorious.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p383/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | One explanation takes definite الحق as an allusion to the established rule in the Prophetic hadith that Muslim blood is protected except in three cases.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p383/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · أبو هريرة | reports | A Prophetic report through Abu Hurayra says the Israelites split five hundred years after Moses when children of captives multiplied, and split again a hundred years after Jesus.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p383/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another explanation identifies the transgression as their violation of the Sabbath prohibition. | mentions 4:154
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p383/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | ما in بما عصوا is a verbal noun marker, so the phrase means because of their disobedience.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p383/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | اعتداء is not coordinated with عصيان to preserve the verse endings and suggest transgression had become their habitual, continual act.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p383/r14] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · صاحب المنتخب | reports | The punishment is explained by causes ordered by gravity: first disbelief in God's signs, then killing prophets, then lesser sins and transgression.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p383/r15] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | prefers | The first causal clause explains humiliation and wrath; the second points to disbelief and killing, mapping the two punishments to those two causes as a balanced luff-and-nashr and avoiding redundancy.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p383/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The definite wording can instead emphasize totality: no right existed, whether recognized by Muslims or anyone else.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p383/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | The second ذلك may repeat the earlier reference to punishment, or point to disbelief and killing; on the latter reading it is neither repetition nor emphasis.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p383/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Prior disobedience and transgression emboldened them to reject signs and kill prophets, since sins pave the way to disbelief.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p383/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The cited verses describe deeds darkening hearts and connect the claim that hearts are veiled to God's curse and their disbelief. | mentions 83:14, 2:88, 4:155
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p383/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Transgression is crossing God's boundary from what is right into falsehood.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p383/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another explanation takes transgression as persistence in disobedience and killing prophets.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p383/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another interpretation maps disobedience to breaking the covenant and transgression to killing many prophets.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p383/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another gloss describes transgression as long-lasting disobedience and persistence in it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p384#2/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الخليل بن أحمد | reports | Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad subsisted on barley flour and fresh water, yet had an exceptionally bright mind and strong body, campaigning one year and making pilgrimage the next.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p384#2/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The Israelites were then told to settle where their request could be met and descend to the source of the foods they wanted.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p384#2/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Their humiliation, poverty, and wrath resulted from rejecting miraculous signs that should have led to faith and killing prophets whose guidance brings worldly honor and salvation; earlier disobedience and transgression led to those acts.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p384#2/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The poet's lines illustrate how small beginnings can stir great consequences, fitting the claim that earlier disobedience grew into disbelief and murder.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p384#2/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · شاعر | reports | A second poetic line says people may underestimate evil even as it grows.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p384/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | They wearied of the provision and asked Moses to intercede for familiar foods; he rebuked them for trading precious, effortless manna and quails for laborious, harmful foods that stole worship time and impaired body and perception.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#10/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | بغير الحق is either a circumstantial phrase describing the killers as acting wrongly, or an adjective to an omitted verbal noun meaning an unlawful killing.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#10/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The final و of عصوا assimilates into the following و because the preceding vowel is fatḥa, with no lengthened vowel to block assimilation; اهتدوا وإن تولوا illustrates the same pattern. | mentions 3:20
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#10/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari asks why the verse adds بغير الحق when prophets could only be killed unlawfully; he answers that the killers themselves had no justifying case against them.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#10/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Another explanation treats بغير الحق as a description of the killing's injustice to the prophets, intensifying the condemnation of the crime.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#10/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The repeated demonstrative ذلك either emphasizes the earlier reference or, with al-Zamakhshari, points specifically to disbelief and killing the prophets as caused by persistent disobedience and transgression.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#10/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | ما is a verbal noun particle and باء is causal, so the clause means because of their disobedience; عصوا is a relative clause with no syntactic case.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#10/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | عصوا derives from عصيوا: the ياء took fatḥa after a vowel change, then was deleted as the first of two quiescent letters, leaving the pattern فعوا.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#10/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | كانوا يعتدون is an accusative predicate of كان, and that clause coordinates with the relative clause of ما.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#10/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | عصيان originally denotes firmness, while اعتداء is تجاوز derived from عدا يعدو; the verse leaves both verbs' objects unstated to include every form of disobedience and transgression.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#10/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | يعتدون originates as يعتديون and undergoes the same deletion and sound change as يتقون, yielding the pattern يفتعون. | mentions 2:21
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#11/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | When a damma before و creates a long vowel, that length blocks assimilation between identical following sounds, so the letters remain distinct, as in آمنوا وعملوا and الذي يوسوس. | mentions 2:25, 2:126
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The standard imperative is ادع with ḍamma; Banu Amir use ادع with kasra.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abu al-Baqa explains the kasra as resolving two adjacent sukuns while treating the weak verb like a sound verb; the author objects that normally the first, not second, of two sukuns is vowelled.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The dialect may instead reflect a verb pattern دعى يدعي like رمى يرمي.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | دعاء here means asking, but can also mean naming or calling, as in the quoted poem دعتني أخاها.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | لنا attaches to ادع, and its lām expresses purpose.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#2/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | يخرج is jussive as the response to the imperative.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#2/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · بعضهم | reports | Some grammarians posit an omitted command lām, understanding ليخرج; al-Zajjaj weakens that analysis.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#3/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · سيبويه | reports | Sibawayh supplies an omitted object for يخرج: مأكولا or شيئا from what the earth grows.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#3/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The preposition من may attach to the verb and mark the point of origin.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#3/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Alternatively, من may qualify the omitted object as something from what the earth grows, with من partitive.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#3/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash treats من as an extra marker in the object, yielding يخرج ما تنبته الأرض; he does not require a special condition for its being extra.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#3/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | ما may be a relative noun or an indefinite noun with an adjective, with its resumptive omitted; it cannot be a verbal noun because the object produced is a concrete substance, not cultivation as an action, under either analysis.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#4/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | من بقلها may be an appositive to ما with the preposition repeated, where من explains the kind.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#4/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | المقثأة and المقثؤة, with fatḥa or ḍamma on tāʾ, name a place where cucumbers grow.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#4/r11] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | الفوم means garlic; fāʾ may irregularly replace thāʾ, as in جدف/جدث, عاثور/عافور, and معاثير/معافير.

4/r12] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عباس | reports | A second interpretation of الفوم is wheat, supported by a verse of poetry Ibn Abbas recited about farming فوم.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#4/r13] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو إسحاق الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj says أدنى derives from دنو, nearness; it can be lower in value and baseness, or nearer to them in this world, while the better food brings afterlife benefit through patience.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#4/r14] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | On the near-in-this-world interpretation, the superior food's benefit is obtained in the afterlife through patience.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#4/r15] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · علي بن سليمان الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash derives أدنى from أدنأ, the lowly or base thing, with hamza softened; the poem is cited as a witness.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#4/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Alternatively it may be an accusative circumstantial phrase describing the omitted pronoun returning to ما; من remains explanatory.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#4/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | بقل is all plant growth without a stem, and its plural is بقول.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#4/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | قثاء is the familiar cucumber; its singular is قثاءة, following the قمح/قمحة pattern.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#4/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · قرئ | reports | The usual pronunciation of قثاء has kasra on qāf, and another reading uses ḍamma.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#4/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The hamza in قثاء is original, as in أقثأت الأرض when cucumbers become abundant; its pattern is فعال.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#4/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | قثاء may have the plural قثائي, like علباء and علابي.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#4/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · بعضهم | reports | Some derive قثاء from a waw-root and cite أقثأت القوم and فثأت القدر; the author calls this a gross error because the expected forms would instead preserve the waw-derived pattern, with yāʾ substitution in the four-letter verb.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#4/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The author rejects that waw-root argument: it should produce أقثيت from أقثوت and فثوت القدر, and the poem should say نفثوها, not نفثؤها.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#5/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The poem fragment is cited with al-Akhfash's proposal that أدنى originated as أدنأ with hamza and underwent hamza easing.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#5/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | In the basic language, المصر is the boundary between two things; people of Hajar used مصورها to mean a property's boundaries, and a poem calls the sun a boundary between day and night.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#5/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · زهير الفرقبي | reports | Zuhayr al-Firqabi reads أدنأ with hamza, supporting the derivation from دنأ and dناءة.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#5/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · قيل | reports | A third etymology takes أدنى from أدون, the bad or inferior thing; the middle radical is moved after the final radical, producing أَدْنَو, then undergoes weak-letter change, on pattern أفلع.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#5/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | أدنى is the predicate of هو, while هو خير is likewise a relative clause with a resumptive element.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#5/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · قرأ الجمهور | reports | The majority read مصر with nunation, matching the written muṣḥaf; one explanation is that they were sent to any Egyptian city, so the word is declinable.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#5/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · قيل | reports | They may instead have been sent to Egypt itself, which is declinable because its middle consonant is silent and the name is light like هند and دعد; a poem illustrates the forms, or the declension may reflect treating it as a place name.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#5/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الحسن وغيره | reports | Al-Hasan and others read مصر without nunation; the same form occurs in some Uthman and Ubayy codices, as if a particular place were intended.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#5/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari says the name is an Arabicized Persian form of مصرائيم; if it names a specific place, its foreignness means it should be indeclinable, like ماه and جور and حمص. | mentions 12:99
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#5/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The majority unanimously prevent declension for مصر in يوسف 12:99. | mentions 12:99
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#6/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | ما is an accusative noun of إن, whose predicate is لكم; it means that which, with its resumptive pronoun omitted: الذي سألتموه.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#6/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الراغب | reports | Al-Raghib says the mīm in مسكنة is extra in the stronger view; citing the dispute also suggests the nūn is extra and the root is مسك.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#6/r11] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The alif in باء is from wāw, as shown by باء يبوء and the pattern قال يقول; باء means to return, and the prophetic wording أبوء بنعمتك علي illustrates it.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#6/r12] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | A poem's آبوا is wrongly offered as evidence for باء: it belongs to آَبَ يَؤوب, with radicals hamza-waw-bāʾ, unlike باء يبوء; reversing the roots is unattested.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#6/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abu al-Baqa regards the indefinite-relative analysis as weak because the request refers to a specific thing, not an unspecified one.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#6/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · قرئ | reports | A reading سلتم, like بعتم, is derived from the long-alif verb سال.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#6/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Hassan's poem سالت هذيل رسول الله witnesses the long-alif form; the origin of its alif is disputed as yāʾ, waw, or hamza, with details deferred to 70:1. | mentions 70:1
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#6/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | ضربت is passive, with الذلة as its نائب الفاعل.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#6/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | ضربت means imposed or decreed upon them, by analogy with erecting tents; al-Farazdaq's poem to Jarir uses ضربت عليك.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#6/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | الذلة means humiliation; ذل with ḍamma is subjection imposed by coercion, while ذل with kasra follows resistance without coercion, as al-Raghib says.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#6/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | مسكنة is on the pattern مفعلة from stillness, since poverty leaves a person with little movement; مسكين follows مفعيل.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#6/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The mīm recurs in تمسكن and متمسكن, but this does not make it a root letter: derivation shows it is extra, as with تمندل and تمذرع.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#7/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | البواء can mean return in retaliation, and people may be بواء, equal in a matter; the poem لا يبوء الدم بالدم means blood is not repaid with blood in retribution.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#7/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · قيل | reports | An alternative attaches من الله directly to the verb, understanding رجعوا من الله بغضب; the author considers this weak.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#7/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | باء بكذا can also mean acknowledge or admit; the cited prophetic report means accepting the favor and binding oneself to it, and poetry uses بؤت بحقها.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#7/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الراغب | reports | Al-Raghib says البواء originally means equal parts sharing one place, contrasted with النبوة, the parts' incompatibility.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#7/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الراغب | reports | Al-Raghib explains باؤوا بغضب as settling in a place with wrath; باء signals that their fitting place carries God's anger, and he compares the ironic announcement in 3:21. | mentions 3:21
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#7/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الراغب | reports | Al-Raghib says interpreting بؤت بحقها as I admitted its right does not follow the word's lexical implication.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#7/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · خلف الأحمر | reports | Khalaf al-Ahmar says حياك الله وبياك originally was بوأك and changed for sound-pattern matching.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#7/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | بغضب is a circumstantial phrase describing those who returned: they returned under wrath, not with wrath as a direct object.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#7/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari reads باء فلان بفلان as deserving to be killed in retaliation for him, hence becoming deserving God's wrath; this makes the bāʾ phrase unlike a circumstantial phrase.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#7/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | من الله most naturally modifies غضب as an adjective, with an implied كائن; من marks metaphorical origin.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#8/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The demonstrative ذلك points back to the humiliation, poverty, and incurring of wrath; the clause بأنهم is its predicate and explains the cause of that fate.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#8/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو عبيد | reports | Abu Ubayd says nearly all readers, ordinary speakers, and most Arabs omit the hamza, and relates a report in which the Prophet corrects a man who says يا نبيء الله.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#8/r11] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abu Ubayda says Arabs replace hamza in النبي، البرية، and الخابية; he adds الذرية from ذرأ, while Sibawayh's تنبأ مسيلمة shows that the hamza is original.
[SAMIN-DURR:2:61#8/r12] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الحاكم | reports | Al-Hakim grades the correction report authentic according to the conditions of the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections, though neither collection includes it.

[BURHAN:v2p346/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | rejects | Al-Zarkashi says this contradicts the rhetoricians’ consensus: the cited questions refer to past actions; no evidence supports future reference, and the grammar of أتقتلون does not determine the intended time.
